solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Lioness licked wounds

indicators.note: to be licked is to be beaten, and a beaten-up word loses its shape and order

blocks.note: the fodder, seven letters taken exactly as printed

explanation.surface: A lioness tending her injuries with her tongue after a fight on the savannah.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants 'licked' to be what the lioness does to her wounds; it is really the instruction to rearrange her letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesions are injuries or damaged patches of tissue, so the plural noun is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Affair exposed in Australia is ongoing

indicators.note: something exposed inside a phrase is laid bare within its run of letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the ends and middle of these three words

explanation.surface: A scandalous romance has come to light in Australia and is still going on.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across the words: austraLIA IS ONgoing.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison is a secret romantic or sexual relationship, which is exactly what an affair means here.

clue.text: Nun’s a poet, so madly impulsive

indicators.note: acting madly means acting without order, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, ignoring the apostrophe and comma

explanation.surface: A nun who writes verse turns out to be surprisingly rash and wild.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive's apostrophe is surface dressing; the fodder is every letter of 'Nun's a poet, so', and the anagram signal sits between it and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spontaneous behaviour is done on a sudden urge without planning, matching impulsive as a synonym.

clue.text: Oscar moved back and forth

indicators.note: going back means travelling the wrong way, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
drawn along, as a cart is moved by a horse

explanation.surface: Someone called Oscar pacing to and fro.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back and forth' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'back' turns the synonym for moved round, 'and' is the link, and 'forth' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Forth and onward both mean forwards in space or time, as in 'from this day forth'.

clue.text: Asteroid affected sailors in front half of ship first

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is held between that other's letters
the front half of a word keeps its opening letters and drops the rest

blocks.note: its front half is the first two of its four letters
tars are sailors
to ape is to put on or affect a manner

explanation.surface: An asteroid has somehow affected the crew at the front of a spaceship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asteroid' is not the space rock here but the adjective: from Greek aster, star, it means shaped like a star. 'First' puts the ship-and-sailors piece before the synonym for affected.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, asteroid is the literal Greek-derived word for having the outline of a star, as starfish do.

clue.text: Sacred place of frenzied Tuscan maidens

indicators.note: a frenzied crowd is wild and disordered, so these letters are thrown about

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A holy shrine where Tuscan girls once danced in religious ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maidens' suggests young women; in cricket a maiden is an over with no runs scored, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: A sanctum is a holy inner chamber of a temple or church, so the phrase is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Erected huge house in part of London

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up makes it read from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing size
a standard abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A huge house has been built in one of London's districts.
explanation.walkthrough: Soho is a district of London's West End, known for theatres, restaurants and nightlife.
explanation.definitionFit: Soho is one district of central London, so the answer is an example of a part of that city.

clue.text: Travelled around with chap who painted sea creatures

indicators.note: turned around means facing the opposite way, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: ran as in a train or bus that travelled a route
W is a standard abbreviation for with
Frans Hals, the Dutch Golden Age portrait painter

explanation.surface: An artist who went round the world with a companion painting marine life.
explanation.walkthrough: Frans Hals painted The Laughing Cavalier; setters use him constantly for HALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Narwhals are Arctic whales with a long spiral tusk, so they are an example of animals that live in the ocean.

clue.text: More than is proper, couple made out

indicators.note: what is made out is caught by ear, as when you make out words in a noisy room

blocks.note: a couple is a pair

explanation.surface: A pair kissed in public more than decency allows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made out' reads as a couple kissing; it is really the signal that what you hear stands for the spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Too means excessively, beyond what is right or desirable, as in 'too loud'.

clue.text: Order male partner for the night

blocks.note: a man is a male
the person you go out with for an evening

explanation.surface: Someone booking a male escort for the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like the verb of the surface, placing a booking; the answer can be a noun or a verb, and both fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandate is an official command or instruction, the same as an order issued by an authority.

clue.text: Names withheld, and no fuss

indicators.note: what is withheld is kept back and not handed over, so it goes missing

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, taken as printed
N is short for name, so names are two of them

explanation.surface: An anonymous arrangement handled quietly without any drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is inside the clue's own words: strip both Ns out of 'and no' and A, D and O remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ado is fuss or bother, as in Much Ado About Nothing, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Rough male sheep reportedly sported

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so we want what the word sounds like, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: a wether is a castrated ram
clothes sported are clothes worn

explanation.surface: A ram with a shaggy, rough fleece, according to the farmer's account.
explanation.walkthrough: A wether is a castrated male sheep, a farming word; it sounds exactly like weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Something weatherworn has been roughened and damaged by exposure to wind and rain, so it is rough.

clue.text: Seated, I get up and take off

blocks.note: sat means seated
taken as printed
to rise is to get up

explanation.surface: A passenger in their seat stands up as the plane takes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' pretends to be an aircraft leaving the ground; it is the sense of mimicking someone to mock them.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is to parody or mimic them for comic effect, which is what satirising does.

clue.text: Dance companion for daughter in Russian cottage

indicators.note: one thing given for another is a swap, the first standing in the second's place

blocks.note: CH is Companion of Honour, a British order
the standard abbreviation
a dacha is a Russian country house

explanation.surface: A girl bringing a dance partner along to a country cottage in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: Replace the D of DACHA with CH, the Companion of Honour, a British award whose initials setters use for companion.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha is a Latin American ballroom routine, so the answer is an example of a dance.

clue.text: Stylish toy boy paid peanuts

blocks.note: chic means stylish
Ken is Barbie's boyfriend, literally a boy who is a toy
fee'd, given a fee

explanation.surface: A fashionable younger lover who is kept on a meagre allowance.
explanation.walkthrough: A toy boy is an older woman's young lover; here it is read literally as Ken, the boy doll sold with Barbie. 'Paid' is split as fee'd, a playful coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: Peanuts and chicken feed are both idioms for a trivially small sum of money.

clue.text: Build on island group after influx of key capital

indicators.note: an influx is a flowing in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to add to something is to build on it
IS is the map abbreviation for island
the Swedish pop group
A is a musical key

explanation.surface: Developers planning to build on a group of islands once money from a major city flows in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group' is the pop group ABBA, and the key A goes into its middle. 'Capital' looks like money but is the definition: Ethiopia's capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Addis Ababa is the capital city of Ethiopia, so the answer is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Fool old lady

blocks.note: British slang for a silly or daft person
an affectionate family name for a grandmother

explanation.walkthrough: Nana as a fool is British slang, probably from banana; the grandmother sense is known everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday informal words: a daft person in British slang, and a child's name for a grandmother.

clue.text: British Airedale angrily biting backside of Cocteau, French poet

indicators.note: something done angrily is done violently, which throws the letters out of order
a mouth biting something closes around it and holds it
the backside is the rear, meaning the final letter of the word

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
eight letters of fodder; an Airedale is a breed of terrier
the last letter of the French writer's surname

explanation.surface: A British terrier savagely biting the French writer Jean Cocteau on the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange AIREDALE as A-DELAIRE and slip the U in after the first A, then put B in front. The dog breed contains most of the poet's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Baudelaire wrote Les Fleurs du mal, so he is a nineteenth-century example of a poet from France.

clue.text: Steam iron briefly dispersed spray

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its final letter off
things dispersed are scattered about, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: fodder taken as printed
the word without its final N

explanation.surface: A steam iron puffing out a fine mist of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spray' could be a verb in the surface; it is the noun, a device, and only the N of the iron is trimmed before rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An atomiser is a device that turns liquid into a fine mist, and spray names both the mist and the device.

clue.text: Experts study glass eye, perhaps

definitions.note: the definition is an example; the answer is the general term

blocks.note: pros are professionals, experts
a thesis is an extended academic study

explanation.surface: Specialists examining someone's artificial eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks the glass eye as one example of the broader answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A prosthesis is any artificial body part, and a glass eye is one such replacement.

clue.text: Reveal boozer is supporting large hospital

indicators.note: in a down clue, what supports another sits below it, so the order is set top to bottom

blocks.note: boozer is British slang for a pub
the clothing-size abbreviation
taken as printed
the map-sign abbreviation

explanation.surface: Exposing that a local pub is propping up a big hospital financially.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'is supporting large' puts IS underneath L. A boozer is a British pub, not a drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: To publish is to make information public, so reveal is a close synonym.

clue.text: Children cycling slip sideways on road

indicators.note: a cycle goes round, so the final letter comes round to the front

blocks.note: kids are children

explanation.surface: Kids on bicycles sliding out of control on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Cycling is both the surface's bike ride and the instruction: move the last letter of KIDS to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A skid is the uncontrolled sliding of a vehicle when its tyres lose grip, as in the definition.

clue.text: Comedian periodically nearly faltering

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: Ken Dodd, the Liverpool comedian famous for his tickling stick
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A comic whose act was, now and then, close to falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Dodd was a long-running British stand-up comedian, the usual crossword comedian for DODD.
explanation.definitionFit: Doddery describes someone shaky and unsteady from old age, which is what faltering suggests.

clue.text: Mostly stick together to protect single or joint beneficiary

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
protecting something means wrapping around it to shield it

blocks.note: cohere without its final E
the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Siblings closing ranks to shield whoever is inheriting, whether alone or with others.
explanation.walkthrough: The I goes between the HE and the R of the shortened verb. 'Or' is an unusual link word, offering the definition as an alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: A coheir is one of several people who inherit an estate together, so a shared beneficiary.

clue.text: Well-endowed, society bores thrive marvellously at last

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into something, so one piece goes inside another
at last points to the very end, the final letter

blocks.note: a business that booms thrives
the standard abbreviation
its final letter

explanation.surface: A wealthy society whose tedious members flourish splendidly in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' reads as dull people but is the verb, drilling S into the synonym for thrive. 'Well-endowed' pretends to mean rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-endowed is a coy idiom for having a large bust, which is what bosomy means.

clue.text: Am returning jumper boy left behind

indicators.note: returning means coming back the way you went, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as printed
a roo, short for kangaroo, is a jumper
Ned is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Coming home to find a jumper a boy forgot.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is British for a sweater, so the surface reads as lost clothing; here it is the kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: To be marooned is to be abandoned somewhere with no way to leave, so stranded or left behind.

clue.text: Object to minute diamonds

blocks.note: the abbreviation for minute
the card-suit abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone complaining about tiny diamonds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' pretends to mean tiny, pronounced my-NEWT; it is the unit of time.
explanation.definitionFit: To mind something is to dislike or object to it, as in 'do you mind if I smoke?'.

clue.text: Look into endowing missing knight with a vacant title

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so it drops out
a vacant word is emptied, keeping only its outside letters

blocks.note: investing someone with a quality is endowing them with it
N is the chess notation for a knight
taken as printed
its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Inquiring into the award of a title that has been left unfilled since a knight disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: The knight is N from chess notation, not Sir or K as a solver might first try, and 'vacant' empties a word to its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To investigate is to examine or inquire into something carefully, so look into is an idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: See case of Italian wine

indicators.note: a case is the outside covering, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: v. for vide, Latin for see, used in references
its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Look at a crate of Italian wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian wine' wants to be the definition, but the answer is French: vin.
explanation.definitionFit: Vin is the French word for wine, familiar from vin rouge and vin blanc on menus.

clue.text: Regularly envied woman

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A woman who is often the object of envy.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is in the odd letters: EnViEd.
explanation.definitionFit: Eve, the first woman in Genesis, is the standard crossword stand-in for any woman.

clue.text: Worms dog, angry-looking figure

blocks.note: Hund is German for dog, and Worms is a German city
red in the face with anger

explanation.surface: A dog with worms, looking furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worms' is not a parasite but the city of Worms on the Rhine, telling you to give the German word for dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A hundred is a number, and figure is a common crossword word for a number.

clue.text: With bitterness, start to admonish councillor doing nothing

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: its first letter
Cllr or Cr, the British abbreviation for councillor
idly means without doing anything

explanation.surface: Sharply beginning to tell off a councillor who is shirking.
explanation.walkthrough: Cr is the short title for a councillor in British local government.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrid means sharp and bitter in taste, smell or manner, so the adverb means with bitterness.
